Combining: Drain the pasta and toss it in the pan with the sauce over medium heat for 1 minute, adding pasta water a splash at a time until it coats every strand.
Serving: Serve immediately with fresh basil leaves and grated parmesan.
makaronia_napoliten.wine: A light red Chianti or a Greek Agiorgitiko without oak.
makaronia_napoliten.plate: Twirl into a nest in the centre of the plate, with basil leaves on top and cheese served alongside.

steps: Flattening the meat: Place each slice between two sheets of cling film and beat it with a mallet or rolling pin to an even 5 mm thickness. Important: even thickness is everything — thin edges burn while thick centres stay raw.
Seasoning: Season both sides with salt and pepper and let the slices sit for 10 minutes.
Setting up the coating: Line up three shallow dishes: flour, beaten eggs, breadcrumbs.
Coating: Dip each slice in flour and shake off the excess, then in egg letting the surplus drip away, then press it firmly into the breadcrumbs.
Resting the coating: Let the coated schnitzels rest for 10 minutes. This lets the crumb bind to the egg, so the crust does not slide off in the pan.
Heating the oil: Heat plenty of oil to 175°C in a wide pan — a crumb dropped in should sizzle immediately without browning instantly.
Frying: Fry for 3-4 minutes per side until deep golden, turning only once. Turning repeatedly breaks the crust.
Not crowding: Fry two at a time at most. Important: a crowded pan drops the oil temperature and the coating soaks up fat instead of crisping.
Draining: Drain on a rack, not on paper — paper traps steam underneath and the bottom crust goes soft.
Serving: Serve immediately with lemon wedges.
snitsel_xoirino.wine: A cold beer, or a crisp white such as Moschofilero.
snitsel_xoirino.plate: Serve one schnitzel per plate covering most of it, with a lemon half and fries or mashed potato on the side.

steps: Cutting the potatoes: Peel the potatoes and cut them into large chunks. Cut them too small and they disintegrate into the sauce.
Sautéing the onion: Sauté the sliced onion in the oil over medium heat for 6-8 minutes, until soft and golden and genuinely sweet.
Adding the paste: Add the garlic and the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, so the paste loses its metallic raw taste.
Sautéing the potatoes: Add the potatoes and turn them in the oil for 3-4 minutes, so their surface seals and they hold their shape.
Adding the tomato: Pour in the grated tomato, the bay leaf and the sugar, and add just enough hot water to barely cover the potatoes.
Simmering: Important: Simmer over low heat without stirring — shake the pot by its handles instead. A spoon breaks the potatoes apart.
Cooking: Cook for about 35 minutes, until the potatoes are soft and the sauce has thickened and turned glossy.
Seasoning: Season with salt and pepper towards the end, once the sauce has reduced and its saltiness has concentrated.
Resting: Scatter over the chopped parsley and let it stand for 10 minutes off the heat — like all yiahni dishes it improves as it settles.
patates_giaxni.wine: A light rosé or a fresh white Roditis.
patates_giaxni.plate: Serve in a deep dish with plenty of sauce, feta on the side and bread for dipping.

ing: Mayonnaise 3 tbsp or olive oil 4 tbsp
steps: Draining the tuna: Drain the tuna well and flake it with a fork into large pieces. Important: draining matters — the tin oil is neutral and would dilute the dressing.
Boiling the eggs: Boil the eggs for 9 minutes for a firm but not chalky yolk, then cool them at once in iced water so they peel cleanly.
Taming the onion: Slice the red onion thinly and soak it in cold water with a little lemon for 10 minutes, to take the harsh bite out of it.
Preparing the greens: Wash the lettuce, dry it thoroughly and tear it by hand into bite-sized pieces. Wet leaves repel the dressing.
Making the dressing: Whisk the mayonnaise or oil with the lemon juice, chopped dill, salt and pepper into a smooth emulsion.
Assembling: Layer the lettuce in a wide bowl, then the tuna, the corn, the halved cherry tomatoes, the drained onion and the capers.
Adding the eggs: Cut the eggs into quarters and arrange them around the edge instead of mixing them in, so they stay whole and presentable.
Dressing: Pour the dressing over only at the moment of serving. Dressed early, the lettuce wilts within minutes.
salata_tonou.wine: A dry white Sauvignon Blanc or a Greek Assyrtiko.
salata_tonou.plate: Serve in a wide shallow bowl with the egg quarters around the rim and dill scattered over the top.

steps: Boiling the pasta: Cook the pasta in well-salted water until just al dente — it firms up further as it cools, so do not overcook it.
Cooling: Important: Drain and rinse it under cold water to stop the cooking, then toss it with a spoonful of oil so it does not clump into a block.
Chopping the vegetables: Cut the cucumber and pepper into small even dice and halve the cherry tomatoes.
Draining the tomatoes: Let the halved tomatoes sit in a sieve with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes, so their juice does not water down the salad later.
Making the dressing: Whisk the oil, vinegar, oregano, salt and pepper until emulsified and slightly thickened.
Combining: Toss the cooled pasta with the vegetables, the olives and half the dressing, and mix gently.
Chilling: Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. Pasta salad needs this time — the pasta absorbs the dressing and the flavours settle together.
Finishing: Just before serving, add the crumbled feta, the fresh basil and the rest of the dressing, and check the seasoning — cold food always needs more salt than it seems.
salata_zymarikon.wine: A chilled rosé or a light white Roditis.
salata_zymarikon.plate: Serve in a wide bowl at cool room temperature, with feta crumbled over the top and basil leaves.

steps: Preparing the vegetables: Finely dice the onion, carrot and celery so they melt into the soup rather than sitting in it as chunks.
Sautéing: Sauté them in the butter over medium heat for 6-7 minutes, until soft and fragrant. This base is what separates a real soup from hot water with pasta.
Adding the stock: Pour in the stock and bring it to a rolling boil.
Toasting the vermicelli: Important: Toast the vermicelli in a dry pan for 2 minutes until lightly golden before adding it. This keeps the strands separate and gives a nutty depth.
Adding the pasta: Add the toasted vermicelli to the boiling stock, stirring immediately so it does not settle into a lump at the bottom.
Cooking: Boil for 5-6 minutes only. Vermicelli is very thin — a minute too long and it disintegrates into the broth.
Seasoning: Season with salt and pepper and add the lemon juice off the heat, for brightness.
Serving: Serve straight away with chopped parsley. Important: on standing the vermicelli keeps absorbing liquid, so a soup left to sit turns into porridge.
soupa_fide.wine: Not applicable — a light soup, best with water or a mild white.
soupa_fide.plate: Serve in a deep bowl with parsley on top and a lemon wedge on the rim.

steps: Cutting the chicken: Slice the chicken breast into thin strips against the grain, all the same size so they cook in the same time.
Marinating: Toss the chicken with 2 tbsp soy sauce and the cornflour and leave it for 15 minutes. The cornflour forms a coating that keeps the meat juicy at high heat.
Preparing everything first: Important: Cut and lay out every vegetable before you turn on the heat. A stir fry takes 8 minutes total and there is no time to chop mid-cooking.
Making the sauce: Mix the remaining soy sauce, the honey, the grated ginger and 3 tbsp water in a small bowl.
Heating the pan: Heat a wok or a wide pan until it is genuinely smoking hot. Important: a lukewarm pan stews the food instead of searing it, and the vegetables go limp.
Cooking the chicken: Add oil and the chicken in a single layer, leave it untouched for 1 minute to colour, then stir-fry for 3 minutes and remove it.
Cooking the vegetables: Add a little more oil and stir-fry the harder vegetables — broccoli and carrot — for 2 minutes, then the peppers for another 2.
Combining: Return the chicken, add the garlic and the sauce and toss everything for 1-2 minutes until the sauce thickens and glazes the ingredients.
Finishing: Off the heat, add the sesame oil, the spring onions and the sesame seeds, and serve immediately.
stir_fry_kotopoulo.wine: An aromatic white — Riesling or Malagousia — or a cold beer.
stir_fry_kotopoulo.plate: Serve over steamed rice in a deep bowl, with sesame seeds and spring onion scattered on top.

steps: Soaking the chickpeas: Important: Soak the dried chickpeas in plenty of water for 18-24 hours. Never use canned or cooked chickpeas — they hold too much water and the falafel disintegrate in the oil.
Draining: Drain them thoroughly and spread them on a towel to dry the surface completely.
Grinding: Blitz the raw chickpeas in a food processor with the onion, garlic and herbs until the texture of coarse sand — not a smooth purée.
Resting the mixture: Chill the mixture for 1 hour. This lets it firm up and hold together when shaped.
Seasoning: Mix in the cumin, ground coriander, salt, pepper and flour, working it in evenly.
Adding the soda: Important: Stir in the baking soda only right before frying. Added early it loses its power and the falafel come out dense instead of light.
Shaping: Form small balls or patties with wet hands, pressing firmly so they hold.
Heating the oil: Heat the oil to 170°C. Test with one falafel first — if it breaks apart, work another spoonful of flour into the mixture.
Frying: Fry for 3-4 minutes until deep brown and crisp, a few at a time so the oil temperature stays up.
Draining: Drain on a rack and serve hot, while the outside is still crisp and the inside steaming.
falafel.wine: A cold beer or a fresh dry white with acidity.
falafel.plate: Serve in a pita with tahini sauce, tomato and onion, or on a platter with tahini and lemon on the side.

steps: Choosing the mince: Use mince with about 20% fat. Lean mince gives dry, crumbly kebabs that fall off the skewer.
Draining the onion: Important: Grate the onion and squeeze it hard in a cloth to remove all its juice. Onion water is the main reason kebabs fall apart on the grill.
Mixing: Combine the mince with the drained onion, the crushed garlic, the parsley, the spices, the breadcrumbs, salt and pepper.
Kneading: Knead the mixture firmly for 5 full minutes, until it turns sticky and pulls together as one mass. This kneading develops the protein that binds the kebab.
Resting: Cover and chill for at least 1 hour, so the fat sets and the flavours penetrate.
Shaping: Shape the mixture around flat skewers with wet hands, pressing tightly and leaving no air pockets — air is where they split.
Chilling again: Chill the shaped kebabs for another 20 minutes before they meet the heat.
Grilling: Grill over high heat for 4-5 minutes per side, turning only once so the crust forms properly.
Resting: Let them rest for 5 minutes off the heat before serving, so the juices settle back in.
kebab_spitiko.wine: A red Agiorgitiko without oak, or a cold beer.
kebab_spitiko.plate: Serve on flatbread with grilled tomato and onion, yoghurt sauce and a sprinkle of sumac or paprika.

steps: Boiling the eggs: Place the eggs in cold water and bring to the boil, then cook for exactly 10 minutes for a fully set yolk.
Cooling: Important: Plunge them straight into iced water for 5 minutes. This stops the cooking, prevents the grey-green ring around the yolk, and makes them peel cleanly.
Peeling: Peel them under running water — the stream gets under the membrane and lifts the shell off in pieces.
Halving: Cut them lengthwise with a knife wiped clean between each cut, so the whites stay neat.
Removing the yolks: Scoop out the yolks into a bowl and set the whites aside on the serving platter.
Making the filling: Mash the yolks with a fork until completely smooth, then mix in the mayonnaise, mustard, lemon juice, dill, salt and pepper.
Checking the texture: The filling should be thick enough to hold its shape when piped. Important: too loose and it will slump out of the whites within minutes.
Filling: Pipe the mixture into the whites with a piping bag for a clean finish, or spoon it in generously.
Garnishing: Dust with paprika and top each half with a caper or a piece of olive.
Chilling: Chill for 30 minutes before serving, so the filling firms up and holds its shape.
avga_gemista.wine: A sparkling wine or a dry white as an appetiser.
avga_gemista.plate: Arrange on a flat platter in neat rows, dusted with paprika and scattered with dill.

steps: Preparing the sausages: Cut the sausages into thick 3 cm rounds. Country sausage with fennel and leek is what makes this dish taste of Pelion.
Browning the sausages: Fry them in the oil over high heat until well browned on all sides, then lift them out. Important: their rendered fat stays in the pan and becomes the backbone of the sauce.
Frying the peppers: Cut the peppers into thick strips and fry them in the same fat for 4-5 minutes, until they blister and soften at the edges.
Removing the peppers: Take the peppers out too, so they do not overcook and dissolve while the sauce simmers.
Making the sauce: Sauté the chopped onion and garlic for 4 minutes, add the tomato paste and cook it for 1 minute.
Deglazing: Pour in the wine and let it evaporate, scraping up everything stuck to the bottom of the pan.
Simmering: Add the grated tomato, the bay leaf and the chilli, and simmer for 15 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Combining: Return the sausages and peppers and simmer together for another 10 minutes, so the flavours marry without the peppers falling apart.
Resting: Take it off the heat and let it stand for 10 minutes. Spetzofai is one of those dishes that tastes better warm than scalding hot.
spetzofai.wine: A robust red — Xinomavro or a Tsantali Rapsani from the same region.
spetzofai.plate: Serve straight from the pan or in a clay dish, with plenty of bread and feta on the side.

steps: Cleaning the tripe: Important: Wash the tripe repeatedly under running water and scrub it with coarse salt and vinegar. This step decides everything — badly cleaned tripe gives an unpleasant smell no amount of cooking will fix.
Blanching: Boil it for 10 minutes in plenty of water, drain it and rinse it, discarding that first water entirely.
Cutting: Cut the blanched tripe into strips about 3 cm wide.
Boiling: Cover with fresh water, add the trotter, the bay leaves and the peppercorns and simmer for 3 hours.
Skimming: Skim the foam off the surface for the first 20 minutes, so the broth stays clear rather than cloudy.
Testing: The tripe is ready when it is completely soft and gelatinous and a piece tears easily between your fingers.
Straining: Strain the broth and keep about 1.5 litres of it — this is the soul of the dish.
Making the roux: Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook for 2 minutes, then whisk in hot broth gradually so no lumps form.
Making the avgolemono: Beat the eggs with the lemon juice, then temper them slowly with hot broth, one ladle at a time, beating constantly. Important: rushing this curdles the eggs instantly.
Combining: Pour the avgolemono back into the pot, stir gently and never let it boil again.
Serving: Serve with a garlic and vinegar sauce (skordostoumbi) and chilli flakes on the table for everyone to season their own bowl.
patsas.wine: Traditionally none — patsas goes with tsipouro or plain water.
patsas.plate: Serve steaming hot in a deep bowl, with vinegar-garlic and chilli flakes on the side.

steps: Making the dough: Mix the flour with a pinch of salt, the olive oil and the raki, then add the water gradually while kneading.
Kneading: Knead for 8-10 minutes until the dough is soft, smooth and no longer sticks to your hands. Important: the raki is what makes the pastry crisp and blistered when fried.
Resting the dough: Cover it and let it rest for 30 minutes. Rested dough rolls out thin without springing back.
Draining the cheese: Important: If the mizithra is wet, drain it in a cloth for an hour. Wet filling tears the dough and leaks out during cooking.
Making the filling: Mash the mizithra with the eggs and the chopped mint until evenly combined.
Rolling out: Roll the dough out thin — about 2 mm — on a floured surface and cut discs about 10 cm across.
Filling: Place a spoonful of filling in the centre of each disc, without overfilling — the classic mistake that bursts them open.
Shaping: Fold them into half-moons and press the edges firmly with a fork, or pleat them by hand into the traditional round open shape.
Cooking: Fry them in hot oil for 2 minutes per side until golden, or bake them at 180°C for 25 minutes brushed with egg.
Serving: Serve warm, drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon.
kalitsounia.wine: A sweet Cretan wine or a small glass of raki.
kalitsounia.plate: Arrange overlapping on a platter, drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon, warm.

steps: Slicing the vegetables: Slice the courgettes and potatoes into thin rounds about 3 mm thick, ideally with a mandoline so they are all identical.

Salting the courgettes: Important: Layer the courgette slices in a colander with salt and leave them for 30 minutes, then pat them dry. Courgettes are mostly water, and this is the only way to stop the boureki turning to soup.
Preparing the pan: Oil a large round pan well and lay two phyllo sheets in the base if you are using them.
First layer: Arrange a layer of potato slices, season, and dust lightly with flour — the flour absorbs the juices released during baking.
Cheese layer: Crumble over some mizithra, sprinkle graviera and scatter chopped mint.
Building up: Continue alternating courgette, potato and cheese in layers, finishing with a layer of vegetables and cheese on top.
Finishing the top: Drizzle generously with olive oil and scatter sesame seeds over the surface.
Baking: Bake at 180°C for 1 hour and 15 minutes, until deep golden and the liquid has fully evaporated.
Checking: Important: If liquid is still bubbling around the edges, keep baking. Boureki cut too soon collapses on the plate.
Resting: Let it rest for at least 30 minutes before cutting. It is traditionally eaten warm, not hot.
boureki_xanion.wine: A fresh Cretan white — Vidiano or Vilana.
boureki_xanion.plate: Cut into large squares and serve warm on a flat plate, with the sesame crust facing up.

steps: Purging the snails: Important: Keep the live snails for 5-7 days in a covered ventilated container with flour or bran, so they empty themselves. This step is not optional for safety.
Washing: Wash them repeatedly in plenty of water with a little vinegar, until the water runs completely clear.
Blanching: Boil them for 5 minutes in salted water, then drain them well.
Drying: Dry them very well and dry the shell openings too. Important: any water left inside will spit violently the moment it hits the hot oil.
Coating with flour: Dip the open face of each snail in flour, tapping off the excess. The flour seals the opening and forms the crust.
Heating the oil: Heat the oil in a wide pan until it is very hot — this dish only works at high heat.
Frying: Place the snails opening-side down into the oil — this is what boubouristi means — and fry them for 2-3 minutes without moving them.
Adding the vinegar: Stand back and pour in the vinegar. It will spit and steam violently. Let it evaporate for 1-2 minutes.
Finishing: Add the rosemary and coarse salt, swirl the pan once and serve immediately while sizzling.
saligkaria_boubouristi.wine: Cretan raki or a robust white wine with acidity.
saligkaria_boubouristi.plate: Serve straight from the pan, opening-side up, with the vinegar sauce and bread to mop it up.

steps: Cleaning the greens: Wash the greens repeatedly in several changes of water until no grit is left at the bottom of the bowl. Wild greens hold far more soil than they look.
Chopping: Chop them coarsely — greens shrink dramatically and finely chopped ones turn to mush.
Sautéing the onions: Sauté the onion and spring onions in the oil over medium heat for 6 minutes, until soft and sweet.
Adding the spices: Important: Add the paprika and the chilli off the heat, or lower it right down. Paprika burns in seconds and turns bitter.
Adding the greens: Add the greens in batches, waiting for each lot to wilt before adding the next, or the pot will overflow.
Adding the fennel: Stir in the chopped wild fennel — this is the herb that gives tsigarelli its Corfiot identity.
Adding the rice: Add the rice and about a cup of hot water, which will thicken the dish as it cooks.
Simmering: Cover and simmer over low heat for 25-30 minutes, until the greens are tender and the liquid has been mostly absorbed.
Finishing: Add the lemon juice off the heat, check the seasoning and let it stand for 10 minutes. It is eaten warm or at room temperature.
tsigarelli.wine: A dry white from Corfu — Kakotrygis — or a fresh Robola.
tsigarelli.plate: Serve in a deep dish with plenty of oil on top, feta on the side and bread.

steps: Desalting the cod: Important: Soak the salt cod for 24-36 hours in the fridge, changing the water 5-6 times. Under-soaked cod is inedibly salty and cannot be corrected later.
Testing: Taste a small piece of the thickest part — it should be pleasantly savoury, not salty.
Cutting: Cut the cod into large portions and remove any large bones with tweezers.
Cleaning the leeks: Slice the leeks into thick rounds and wash them thoroughly between the layers, where soil always hides.
Sautéing the leeks: Sauté the leeks and the onion in the oil over medium heat for 10 minutes, until they collapse and sweeten. This slow start is what makes the dish.
Adding the paste: Stir in the tomato paste and cook it for 1 minute, then add the grated tomato, the bay leaf and the sugar.
Simmering the sauce: Simmer for 20 minutes until the leeks are completely soft and the sauce has thickened.
Adding the cod: Lay the cod pieces on top of the sauce without stirring, cover and cook for 15 minutes only. Important: cod falls apart quickly, so it goes in last and is never stirred.
Seasoning: Season with pepper only — the cod brings its own salt. Taste before adding any.
Resting: Scatter over parsley and let it rest for 10 minutes off the heat before serving.
bakaliaros_prasa.wine: A dry white with acidity — Assyrtiko or Robola.
bakaliaros_prasa.plate: Serve the cod pieces whole on a bed of leeks in a deep plate, with sauce spooned over and bread.

steps: Break the biscuits by hand into uneven pieces. Important: do not crush them to crumbs — the visible chunks are what give this dessert its character.
Beat the soft butter with the icing sugar and cocoa until light and smooth.
Add the milk and brandy gradually, beating until you have a glossy cream.
Fold in the biscuits and chopped walnuts by hand, coating every piece without breaking them further.
Tip the mixture onto cling film and roll it into a tight log, twisting the ends closed.
Important: Refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Cut too early it collapses, because the butter has not set.
Slice into thick rounds with a knife dipped in hot water for clean edges.
glyko_psygeiou.wine: A sweet wine or a double espresso.
glyko_psygeiou.plate: Serve in thick rounds on a white plate, with the biscuit pieces visible in the cut.

steps: Chill the cream, the bowl and the whisk in the freezer for 10 minutes — cold equipment is what lets cream whip properly.
Whip the cream to soft peaks, stopping before it turns grainy.
In a separate bowl mix the condensed milk with the lemon zest.
Important: Add the lemon juice slowly while stirring. The acid thickens the condensed milk on contact, and pouring it in at once creates lumps that never smooth out.
Fold the lemon mixture into the whipped cream with a spatula, using gentle upward strokes to keep the air in.
Divide into glasses and refrigerate for at least 4 hours until set.
Serve chilled with a little extra zest on top.
mous_lemoniou.wine: A Muscat of Lemnos or a sweet sparkling wine.
mous_lemoniou.plate: Serve in clear glasses with lemon zest and a mint leaf.

steps: Dissolve the jelly powder completely in the hot water, stirring until no grains remain on the bottom.
Add the cold water and let the mixture cool to room temperature.
Important: Never use fresh pineapple, kiwi or papaya. They contain enzymes that break down gelatine, and the jelly will never set.
Cut the fruit into even pieces and dry them lightly on kitchen paper.
Pour a thin layer of jelly into the mould and refrigerate for 30 minutes until just tacky.
Arrange the fruit on this set layer — this stops everything sinking to the bottom — and pour over the rest of the jelly.
Refrigerate for at least 4 hours. To unmould, dip the base in warm water for 5 seconds only.
zele_frouta.wine: Juice or sparkling water with lemon.
zele_frouta.plate: Turn out onto a platter so the fruit shows through the clear jelly.

steps: Important: The cream must be ice cold, straight from the fridge. Warm cream will not hold air, and without air the result is a frozen block rather than ice cream.
Whip the cream on high speed until firm peaks form and the whisk leaves clear tracks.
Fold in the condensed milk in three additions, with a spatula and gentle upward strokes.
Stop as soon as the mixture is uniform. Over-mixing knocks out the air you just whipped in.
Pour into a container, smooth the top and cover the surface directly with cling film so ice crystals cannot form.
Freeze for at least 6 hours. No churning and no stirring is needed — the sugar in the condensed milk keeps it scoopable.
Take it out 5 minutes before serving so it softens just enough to scoop.
pagoto_spitiko.wine: A liqueur, or espresso for an affogato.
pagoto_spitiko.plate: Serve in scoops in a chilled bowl, with chocolate or fruit on top.

ing: Dulce de leche or condensed milk 400 g
steps: Crush the biscuits to fine crumbs and mix them with the melted butter until they look like wet sand.
Press the mixture firmly into a tart tin, base and sides, using the back of a glass to compact it evenly.
Refrigerate the base for 30 minutes to set. Important: an unchilled base crumbles the moment you cut the first slice.
Spread the dulce de leche over the base in an even layer.
Slice the bananas and arrange them over the caramel, overlapping slightly.
Important: Toss the banana slices in a little lemon juice first, or they will darken and look unappetising within the hour.
Whip the cream with the icing sugar to firm peaks and spread it over the bananas in generous swirls.
Grate dark chocolate over the top and refrigerate for 2 hours before serving.
banoffee.plate: Cut into portions with a hot knife so the three layers show cleanly.

steps: Mix the crushed biscuits with the melted butter and press them into the base of a springform tin.
Freeze the base for 20 minutes so it is solid before the ice cream goes on.
Important: Soften the ice cream in the fridge for 15 minutes, not on the counter and never in the microwave. Half-melted ice cream refreezes with ice crystals and loses its texture.
Spread the vanilla ice cream over the base in an even layer and return it to the freezer for 1 hour.
Spread the chocolate ice cream over the frozen first layer and freeze for another 2 hours.
Heat the cream, pour it over the chopped chocolate and stir until you have a smooth glossy ganache.
Important: Let the ganache cool to room temperature before pouring it over. Warm ganache melts a channel straight through the layers.
Pour it over the cake, scatter the toasted almonds and freeze for a final 2 hours.
Move it to the fridge 15 minutes before serving and cut with a hot knife.
tourta_pagoto.plate: Serve in slices showing the layers, with the ganache running down the edges.

steps: Beat the yolks with the sugar over a bain-marie for about 8 minutes, until pale, thick and warm to the touch.
Important: The bowl must never touch the water and the heat must stay low, or the yolks scramble and the mixture is ruined.
Take it off the heat and keep beating until it has cooled completely to room temperature.
Whip the cream separately to soft peaks — softer than for a cake, because it stiffens further in the freezer.
Fold the cream into the cooled yolk mixture in three additions, gently, keeping as much air as possible.
Fold in the chopped hazelnuts and grated chocolate.
Line a loaf tin with cling film, leaving a generous overhang, and pour in the mixture.
Freeze for at least 6 hours. Unlike ice cream, semifreddo needs no churning — the whipped air is what keeps it soft.
Turn it out using the cling film and slice while still frozen, then let the slices stand for 5 minutes before serving.
semifredo.plate: Cut into slices and serve with toasted hazelnuts and chocolate sauce.

steps: Chop the chocolate finely and even — large lumps do not melt fully and leave the ganache grainy.
Heat the cream to just below boiling, until small bubbles form at the edges, and never let it boil.
Pour the hot cream over the chocolate and leave it for 2 minutes without touching it, so the heat spreads evenly.
Stir from the centre outwards in small circles until the ganache turns glossy and smooth.
Important: If the mixture splits and looks oily, add a tablespoon of cold cream and beat hard — this brings it back together.
Stir in the butter and the brandy and refrigerate for 3 hours until firm enough to shape.
Roll into balls with cool hands, working quickly so the ganache does not melt against your palms.
Roll each one in cocoa or ground biscuits and refrigerate for another hour before serving.
troufakia.wine: Brandy or a sweet red wine.
troufakia.plate: Serve in paper cases on a platter, dusted with cocoa.

steps: Take everything out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Important: cold yogurt and eggs make the batter split, and a split batter bakes heavy and dense.
Beat the eggs with the sugar for 5 minutes, until pale and tripled in volume.
Add the oil in a slow stream while beating, so it emulsifies rather than sitting on the surface.
Fold in the yogurt, the vanilla and the lemon zest.
Sift the flour with the baking powder and soda, and fold it in with a spatula in three additions.
Important: Stop mixing the moment no dry flour remains. Beating flour develops gluten, and gluten makes cake rubbery.
Pour into a buttered and floured tin and bake at 175°C for 45-50 minutes.
Test with a skewer in the centre — it should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack so the base does not steam and go soggy.
keik_giaourtiou.plate: Serve in slices with icing sugar and a little honeyed yogurt alongside.

steps: Drain the pineapple rings thoroughly and pat them dry on kitchen paper. Important: wet fruit dilutes the caramel and it never sets.
Melt the 60 g of butter with the brown sugar in the tin over low heat until bubbling and syrupy.
Arrange the pineapple rings on the caramel, with a cherry in the centre of each — remember the whole thing gets turned over, so this is your final surface.
Beat the butter with the sugar until light, then add the eggs one at a time.
Fold in the sifted flour and baking powder alternately with the milk, finishing with flour.
Pour the batter gently over the fruit, spreading it without disturbing the arrangement underneath.
Bake at 175°C for 45 minutes, until a skewer in the centre comes out clean.
Important: Turn it out after exactly 5-10 minutes. Sooner and it falls apart; later and the caramel sets like glue and the fruit stays in the tin.
Place the serving plate over the tin, turn it over in one confident movement and lift the tin away.
keik_ananas.wine: A sweet white wine or rum.
keik_ananas.plate: Serve caramel-side up, slightly warm, with whipped cream.

steps: Preheat the oven properly to 200°C. Important: muffins need a hot start — that initial blast is what gives them their domed top.
Mix all the dry ingredients in one bowl: flour, cocoa, sugar, baking powder and salt.
Whisk all the wet ingredients in another bowl: eggs, milk, oil and vanilla.
Important: Pour the wet into the dry and stir 10-12 times only, with a spoon. The batter should stay lumpy — this is the golden rule of muffins.
Fold in the chocolate chips with two or three more turns, no more.
Divide into paper cases, filling them three quarters full so they have room to dome.
Bake at 200°C for 5 minutes, then lower to 180°C for another 15 minutes.
That temperature drop is what makes the top rise sharply and then cook through without burning.
Cool on a rack for 10 minutes before eating, so the chocolate chips set.
mafin_sokolatas.plate: Serve in their paper cases in a basket, slightly warm.

steps: Have the butter, eggs and milk at room temperature — cold ingredients will not emulsify and the batter splits.
Beat the butter with the sugar for 5 full minutes, until genuinely white and fluffy. This long beating is what makes cupcakes light.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each so the mixture stays smooth.
Fold in the sifted flour with the baking powder alternately with the milk, ending with flour.
Fill the cases two thirds full — cupcakes should stay flat on top for the cream, not domed like muffins.
Bake at 175°C for 20-22 minutes and cool them completely on a rack.
Important: The cakes must be stone cold before decorating. On even slightly warm cupcakes the buttercream melts and slides straight off.
For the cream, beat the butter alone for 5 minutes, then add the sifted icing sugar in three additions.
Important: Sift the icing sugar without exception. Unsifted lumps block the piping nozzle at the worst possible moment.
Add the milk a spoonful at a time until pipeable, then pipe swirls onto the cold cupcakes.
cupcakes_voutyrokrema.plate: Serve on a cupcake stand with the buttercream piped high and sprinkles on top.

steps: Use cold butter straight from the fridge, cut into cubes.
Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs, working fast so it does not warm up.
Important: The butter must stay cold. Melted butter makes the pastry hard and greasy instead of crumbly.
Add the sugar, eggs, baking powder, vanilla and zest and bring it together into a dough without kneading it.
Wrap it in cling film and refrigerate for 1 hour. Cold dough rolls out easily and holds its shape in the oven.
Press two thirds of the dough into a tart tin, base and sides, with your fingers.
Spread the jam evenly, leaving a clear margin at the edge so it does not boil over and burn.
Roll the remaining dough into strips and lay them in a lattice over the jam.
Bake at 180°C for 40 minutes, until the lattice is golden and the jam is bubbling gently.
Important: Let it cool completely before cutting. Hot jam runs everywhere and the slices lose their shape.
pasta_flora.wine: A sweet wine or Greek coffee.
pasta_flora.plate: Cut into diamonds so the lattice shows, and serve at room temperature.

steps: Peel the apples, cut them into small cubes and toss them at once with the lemon juice so they do not brown.
Mix in the sugar, cinnamon, raisins and chopped walnuts.
Important: Let the filling stand in a sieve for 20 minutes and discard the juice it releases. This liquid is exactly what turns the pastry to mush.
Toast the breadcrumbs in a little butter until golden — they sit under the filling and absorb any remaining moisture.
Lay out a sheet of phyllo, brush it with melted butter and repeat, stacking all six sheets.
Scatter the toasted breadcrumbs along one long edge and pile the filling on them, leaving a clear border all around.
Fold the two short sides inwards first, then roll it up firmly like a Swiss roll, without gaps.
Place it seam-side down on a lined tray, brush the surface generously with butter and score it in portions.
Bake at 180°C for 40-45 minutes, until deep golden and crisp.
Rest for 15 minutes, then dust with icing sugar and cut along the scored lines.
milopita_rolo.plate: Serve in warm slices, dusted with icing sugar and a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

steps: Beat the eggs well, then add the orange juice, the olive oil and the brandy.
Add the flour gradually and knead for 10 minutes into a soft, elastic dough that no longer sticks.
Cover it and let it rest for 1 hour. Important: without this rest the dough springs back and can never be rolled thin enough.
Roll it out paper thin, so thin you can almost see your hand through it. This is the whole secret of diples.
Cut into long strips about 8 cm wide.
Heat plenty of oil to 180°C in a deep pan — diples must float freely, not touch the bottom.
Important: Dip one end of a strip into the oil, and as it starts to bubble roll it up with two forks. You have about 3 seconds before it stiffens.
Fry for 30-40 seconds until pale gold, no darker — they keep colouring after they come out.
Drain them well on a rack and let them cool completely.
Boil the honey with the water for 3 minutes, dip the cold diples in briefly and lift them straight out.
Important: Cold diples into hot syrup. If both are hot they go soggy and lose their crispness.
Scatter with chopped walnuts and cinnamon and serve.
diples.plate: Stack on a platter with honey, walnuts and cinnamon over each layer.

steps: Make the syrup first: boil the sugar, water, lemon and cinnamon for 8 minutes, then set it aside to cool completely.
Important: The syrup must be cold and the touloumbes hot. This contrast is what lets them absorb syrup without going soggy.
Bring the water and butter to the boil, then tip in the flour and semolina all at once.
Stir vigorously over the heat for 3-4 minutes, until the dough comes away from the sides and forms a ball.
Let it cool for 15 minutes. Important: adding eggs to hot dough cooks them into scrambled lumps.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating hard after each until the dough is smooth and glossy again.
Pipe 6 cm lengths through a star nozzle straight into oil at 160°C — a lower temperature than usual, so they cook through inside.
Fry slowly for 6-8 minutes, turning them, until deep golden all over. Rushing this leaves them raw in the middle.
Lift them straight from the oil into the cold syrup and leave them for 1 minute.
Drain them on a rack and serve with cinnamon.
touloumpes.plate: Serve on a platter with the syrup glistening and a dusting of cinnamon.

steps: Grind the biscuits and the walnuts together to a coarse crumb, keeping a little texture.
Boil the sugar with the water for 3 minutes into a light syrup and let it cool slightly.
Mix the cocoa and the melted butter into the syrup until smooth.
Combine with the biscuit and walnut mixture and the brandy, working it into a firm paste.
Important: If it is too soft to shape, refrigerate it for 30 minutes rather than adding more biscuit, which would make it dry.
Shape into small cylinders about 5 cm long and chill them for 1 hour until solid.
Melt the chocolate over a bain-marie with the spoonful of oil, which gives the coating its shine and stops it cracking.
Important: Never let a drop of water reach the melting chocolate. Even a splash seizes it into a stiff grainy mass that cannot be saved.
Dip each cylinder with a fork, let the excess drip off and set them on parchment.
Refrigerate for 1 hour until the coating is firm and snaps when bitten.
karioka.wine: Brandy or a sweet red wine.
karioka.plate: Serve in paper cases, chilled, with the chocolate snapping as you bite.

steps: Wash the sour cherries and remove the stones with a pitter, keeping the fruit as whole as possible.
Layer the cherries with the sugar in a bowl and leave them overnight in the fridge.
Important: This overnight rest draws the juice out slowly, so the fruit stays whole instead of collapsing during boiling.
Next day, tip everything into a wide pot with the water and bring it to the boil.
Skim the foam off carefully — leaving it in makes the syrup cloudy and shortens how long it keeps.
Boil over medium heat for about 25 minutes, shaking the pot rather than stirring, so the cherries stay intact.
Important: Test the syrup on a cold plate. A drop should hold its shape without spreading, but stop before it feels sticky — overcooked syrup crystallises in the jar.
Add the lemon juice in the last 2 minutes. Its acid prevents crystallisation and brightens the colour.
Let it cool completely and store in sterilised jars.
Serve chilled, by the spoonful, with a glass of cold water alongside.
glyko_vyssino.plate: Serve a spoonful on a small saucer with a glass of cold water alongside.

steps: Pick the walnuts while still green and soft enough for a needle to pass right through.
Important: Wear gloves throughout. Green walnuts stain hands deep brown for days.
Peel the outer skin and pierce each walnut in several places with a needle.
Soak them in fresh water for 6-7 days, changing the water twice a day, until the bitterness is gone.
Important: Do not shorten this soaking. Insufficiently soaked walnuts stay bitter and no amount of syrup will cover it.
Boil them for 15 minutes in clean water, then drain them well.
Boil the sugar with the water, the cloves and the cinnamon into a syrup.
Add the walnuts and simmer over low heat for about 1 hour, until they are dark, glossy and tender.
Add the lemon juice at the end to prevent crystallisation.
Let the sweet stand for 24 hours before jarring, so the walnuts absorb the syrup fully.
glyko_karydaki.plate: Serve one walnut on a saucer with a little syrup and cold water alongside.

steps: Stir the tahini thoroughly in its jar first — the oil always separates and sits on top.
Boil the sugar with the water and the honey to 118°C, the soft-ball stage.
Important: Use a thermometer. Below 115°C the halva never sets; above 125°C it turns hard and brittle.
Warm the tahini gently to about 40°C, so the two mixtures combine without shocking each other.
Pour the hot syrup into the tahini in a thin stream while stirring steadily.
Important: Stir only until just combined. Over-stirring makes the tahini release its oil and the halva turns greasy.
Fold in the toasted nuts, the vanilla and the cinnamon with a few turns.
Pour into a tin lined with cling film and press the surface flat.
Refrigerate for at least 4 hours until fully set.
Cut into cubes and keep in the fridge, where it holds for two weeks.
halvas_tahini.plate: Cut into cubes and serve on a wooden board with nuts scattered around.

steps: Boil the sugar with 300 ml of the water and the lemon juice to 115°C.
Important: The lemon juice is essential — without acid the sugar crystallises and the loukoumi turns grainy instead of soft.
Dissolve the cornflour in the remaining cold water, whisking until no lumps remain.
Pour the cornflour mixture into the hot syrup in a thin stream, whisking hard and continuously.
Important: Now cook over very low heat for 60-75 minutes, stirring often. This long slow cooking is what makes it chewy — there is no shortcut.
The mixture is ready when it turns translucent, deep gold and pulls away from the pan in a thick mass.
Stir in the rose water, the colouring and the pistachios at the very end.
Pour into a tin dusted with cornflour and leave it at room temperature for 12 hours — never in the fridge, which makes it weep.
Cut into cubes with an oiled knife and roll them in a mixture of icing sugar and cornflour.
Store in a tin between layers of the same dusting mixture.
loukoumia.plate: Serve on a platter dusted with icing sugar, with a glass of water alongside.

steps: Drain the mizithra in a cloth for 2 hours if it is at all wet.
Important: Wet mizithra never sets and the melopita comes out of the oven as a soft puddle.
Press the pastry base into a round tin and prick it all over with a fork so it does not puff up.
Pass the mizithra through a sieve or beat it until completely smooth with no lumps.
Warm the honey slightly so it flows, then beat it into the cheese.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each, and finally the flour.
Important: Do not over-beat. Too much air makes the filling rise dramatically and then collapse and crack as it cools.
Pour the filling into the base and smooth the surface.
Bake at 170°C for 50-60 minutes, until set at the edges with a slight wobble in the centre.
Let it cool completely in the tin, dust generously with cinnamon and serve at room temperature.
melopita_sifnou.plate: Serve in pieces at room temperature, with plenty of cinnamon on top.

steps: Use genuinely stale bread, two or three days old. Important: fresh bread turns to paste — stale bread has dried out and drinks the custard instead.
Cut it into thick cubes and spread them in a buttered dish.
Warm the milk with the butter until the butter has melted, without letting it boil.
Beat the eggs with the sugar, the vanilla, the cinnamon and the nutmeg.
Important: Pour the warm milk into the eggs slowly while whisking. Tipping it in at once cooks the eggs into strands.
Pour the custard over the bread and scatter the raisins between the cubes.
Press the bread down gently and leave it for 30 minutes to soak right through.
Bake at 175°C for 45 minutes in a bain-marie — a roasting tin with hot water — which keeps the custard from splitting.
Check by inserting a knife near the centre: it should come out clean, with the surface golden.
Rest for 15 minutes and serve warm, on its own or with a spoonful of cream.
poutinga_psomiou.wine: A sweet wine or warm milk.
poutinga_psomiou.plate: Serve warm in a deep dish with a spoonful of cream.

steps: Heat the milk with the vanilla until just below boiling, then take it off the heat and let it infuse for 10 minutes.
Beat the yolks with the sugar and the cornflour until pale and completely smooth.
Important: Pour the hot milk over the yolks slowly, in a thin stream, whisking without stopping. This tempering is the only thing standing between you and scrambled eggs.
Return the mixture to the pan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly and reaching into the corners of the pan.
Important: Keep whisking especially where the base meets the sides — this is where cream always catches and burns first.
When it thickens, let it bubble for exactly 1 minute more. This cooks out the raw starch taste, which otherwise stays.
Take it off the heat and beat in the butter, which gives it shine and a silkier texture.
Pass it through a sieve if any lumps have formed — this rescues almost any cream.
Cover the surface directly with cling film so no skin forms, and refrigerate for at least 3 hours.
Before using, beat it briefly with a whisk to loosen it back to a smooth cream.
krema_zaxaroplastikis.wine: Not applicable — a base for other desserts.
krema_zaxaroplastikis.plate: Use as a filling, or serve in small glasses with fruit and a biscuit.

steps: Choose ripe but firm fruit — overripe fruit has lost the pectin that makes jam set.
Wash, hull and cut the fruit into even pieces.
Layer it with the sugar in a bowl and leave it for 4 hours or overnight, until the juice runs freely.
Important: This maceration means less boiling later, so the fruit keeps its colour and fresh flavour instead of tasting cooked.
Transfer everything to a wide shallow pot. A wide pot evaporates faster and needs far less cooking time than a deep one.
Bring it to the boil and skim the foam carefully off the top.
Boil over medium-high heat for 20-30 minutes, stirring so it does not catch on the base.
Important: Test on a plate chilled in the freezer — a drop should wrinkle when you push it with a finger. If it runs, keep boiling.
Add the lemon juice in the last 3 minutes: its pectin and acid help it set and keep it from crystallising.
Jar it boiling hot in sterilised jars, seal at once and turn them upside down for 5 minutes to create the vacuum.
spitiki_marmelada.plate: Serve in a glass jar with a wooden spoon, next to fresh bread and butter.

steps: Preparing the ingredients: Take the butter, eggs and milk out of the fridge 1 hour ahead. Important: cold ingredients do not emulsify and the batter splits, baking heavy and dense.
Preparing the tin: Butter the tin and dust it with cocoa rather than flour, so no white marks show on the dark cake.
Beating the butter: Beat the butter with the sugar for 5 full minutes, until pale and fluffy. This is where the cake gets most of its lightness.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each. If the mixture starts to curdle, add a spoonful of the flour to bring it back.
Sifting the dry ingredients: Sift the flour, cocoa, baking powder and salt together twice. Cocoa lumps never dissolve later and leave bitter pockets.
Combining: Fold the dry ingredients in alternately with the milk, in three additions, starting and finishing with flour.
Important: Stop mixing the moment no dry flour is visible. Beating flour develops gluten, and gluten turns cake rubbery.
Baking: Pour into the tin, level the surface and bake at 175°C for 45 minutes.
Testing: Insert a skewer in the centre — it should come out with a few moist crumbs. Wet batter means it needs 5-10 minutes more.
Cooling: Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack so the base does not steam and go soggy.
keik_sokolatas.wine: A sweet red Mavrodaphne or an espresso.
keik_sokolatas.plate: Serve in slices dusted with icing sugar and a scoop of vanilla ice cream alongside.

steps: Zesting the lemons: Zest the lemons before juicing them, taking only the yellow layer. Important: the white pith underneath is bitter and that bitterness carries right through the cake.
Beating the eggs: Beat the eggs with the sugar for 5 minutes, until pale and tripled in volume.
Adding the oil: Pour the olive oil in a thin steady stream while beating, so it emulsifies instead of floating on top.
Adding the yogurt: Fold in the yogurt, the zest and half the lemon juice.
Sifting: Sift the flour with the baking powder and fold it in with a spatula in three additions.
Important: Fold, do not beat. Once flour meets liquid, every extra turn makes the crumb tougher.
Baking: Pour into a buttered and floured tin and bake at 175°C for 40-45 minutes.
Piercing: Straight out of the oven, pierce the hot cake all over with a skewer.
Important: Pour the remaining lemon juice over while the cake is still hot. A hot crumb drinks the juice; a cold one lets it run off the sides.
Glazing: Mix the icing sugar with a little lemon juice into a thick glaze and pour it over the cooled cake so it runs down the sides.
keik_lemoniou.wine: A Muscat or a sweet sparkling wine.
keik_lemoniou.plate: Serve in slices with the lemon glaze running down the sides and zest on top.

steps: Preparing the oranges: Zest the oranges first, then juice them. Important: use freshly squeezed juice — bottled juice is pasteurised and has lost the aromatics that make this cake.
Beating the eggs: Beat the eggs with the sugar for 6 minutes, until very pale and thick enough to leave a ribbon trail.
Adding the oil: Add the olive oil slowly while beating continuously.
Adding the juice: Fold in the orange juice and the zest gently.
Sifting: Sift the flour with the baking powder and salt and fold it in with a spatula.
Important: The batter will look thinner than usual — this is correct. The extra juice is what makes the cake so moist.
Baking: Pour into a buttered tin and bake at 180°C for 45 minutes.
Important: Do not open the oven door during the first 30 minutes. The sudden temperature drop makes the risen centre collapse.
Testing: Test with a skewer in the centre, which should come out clean.
Cooling: Cool for 10 minutes in the tin, then turn out and dust with icing sugar once completely cold.
keik_portokaliou.wine: Vin santo or an orange liqueur.
keik_portokaliou.plate: Serve with fresh orange slices alongside and a little zest on top.

steps: Choosing the bananas: Use bananas whose skins have turned brown and spotted. Important: underripe bananas have no aroma and not enough sugar — this is the single thing that decides the cake.
Mashing: Mash them with a fork, leaving a few small lumps for texture rather than pureeing them smooth.
Beating the butter: Beat the soft butter with the sugar for 4 minutes until light.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, then fold in the mashed bananas.
Sifting: Sift the flour with the baking soda, baking powder, cinnamon and salt.
Important: The soda reacts with the acidity of the bananas and starts working immediately. From this point on, work fast and get it into the oven.
Combining: Fold the dry ingredients in with a spatula in a few turns only, then add the walnuts.
Baking: Pour into a lined loaf tin and bake at 175°C for 50-55 minutes.
Checking: If the top browns too early, cover it loosely with foil and carry on baking.
Cooling: Let it cool completely before slicing — banana cake is fragile while warm and tears apart.
keik_bananas.wine: Filter coffee or a glass of milk.
keik_bananas.plate: Serve in thick slices, slightly warm, with butter or peanut butter.

steps: Grating the carrots: Grate the carrots finely, not coarsely. Important: thick shreds stay hard and crunchy in the finished cake instead of melting into it.
Draining: Squeeze the grated carrot lightly in your hands to remove excess juice, without drying it out completely.
Beating the eggs: Beat the eggs with the sugar for 5 minutes until pale and thickened.
Adding the oil: Pour in the olive oil in a thin stream while beating.
Adding the carrots: Fold in the carrots and the chopped walnuts.
Sifting the spices: Sift the flour with the baking powder, soda, cinnamon and nutmeg, so the spices spread evenly rather than clumping.
Combining: Fold the dry ingredients in with a spatula until just incorporated.
Baking: Bake at 175°C for 50-55 minutes.
Important: Let the cake cool completely before frosting. Cream cheese frosting melts on contact with a warm surface and slides straight off.
Frosting: Beat the cream cheese with the icing sugar until smooth, spread it over the cold cake and scatter walnuts on top.
keik_karotou.wine: Earl Grey tea or a sweet wine.
keik_karotou.plate: Serve with cream cheese frosting spread over and chopped walnuts.

steps: Preparing the ingredients: Have everything at room temperature, especially the butter and the eggs.
Beating the butter: Beat the butter with the sugar for 5 minutes until white and fluffy.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition.
Making the base batter: Sift in the flour with the baking powder and salt, folding it in alternately with the milk.
Splitting the batter: Divide the batter into two bowls, keeping them as equal as you can.
Making the chocolate half: Sift the cocoa into one bowl with a tablespoon of warm milk, so the mixture stays as soft as the plain one.
Important: The two batters must be the same consistency. If one is stiffer, it will not swirl and you get separate layers instead of marbling.
Layering: Spoon the two batters alternately into the tin, in dollops, like a chessboard.
Important: Draw a knife through the batter in one single figure-of-eight movement. More stirring blends the colours into muddy brown and destroys the pattern.
Baking: Bake at 175°C for 50 minutes and cool in the tin for 10 minutes before turning out.
marble_cake.plate: Cut into slices so the marbled pattern shows and serve on a white plate.

steps: Preparing the strawberries: Wash and hull the strawberries and cut them into small pieces.
Drying: Spread them on kitchen paper and dry them thoroughly. Important: wet strawberries release juice into the batter and leave a raw, gummy streak through the cake.
Flouring the fruit: Toss the pieces in a tablespoon of the measured flour. This coating stops them sinking to the bottom during baking.
Beating the butter: Beat the butter with the sugar for 4 minutes, then add the eggs one at a time.
Adding the yogurt: Fold in the yogurt and the vanilla.
Sifting: Sift the remaining flour with the baking powder and salt and fold it in with a spatula.
Adding the fruit: Fold in the floured strawberries with two or three turns only, so they do not break up and colour the whole batter pink.
Baking: Pour into a lined tin and bake at 175°C for 45-50 minutes.
Important: Test with a skewer between the fruit, not through a strawberry, or the moist fruit will make you think the cake is underbaked.
Cooling: Cool completely in the tin — this cake is very moist and breaks apart if turned out warm.
keik_fraoulas.plate: Serve with fresh strawberries and whipped cream on the side.

steps: Preparing the apples: Peel one apple and grate it, and cut the other into small cubes. The grated one adds moisture, the cubes add texture.
Preventing browning: Toss both at once with the lemon juice, or they will oxidise and turn grey within minutes.
Beating the eggs: Beat the eggs with the sugar for 5 minutes until pale and thick.
Adding the oil: Add the olive oil in a thin stream, then fold in the yogurt.
Sifting: Sift the flour with the baking powder and the cinnamon.
Combining: Fold the dry ingredients in with a spatula, then add the apples.
Important: The batter is thick — do not add liquid to loosen it. The apples release plenty of juice as they bake and the cake ends up very moist.
Topping: Pour into the tin and scatter the brown sugar mixed with a little cinnamon over the surface, which forms a light crust.
Baking: Bake at 175°C for 50 minutes.
Important: Test at the centre, avoiding a piece of apple. Moist fruit reads as raw batter on the skewer and leads to overbaking.
keik_milou_me_kanela.plate: Serve warm, dusted with cinnamon and a spoonful of cream.

steps: Preparing the oranges: Zest the oranges before juicing them, taking only the coloured layer.
Beating the butter: Beat the soft butter with the sugar for 5 minutes, until pale and creamy.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, then the orange juice, zest and vanilla.
Important: The mixture will look split at this point. This is normal — the flour brings it back together.
Adding the flour: Sift the flour with the baking powder and add it gradually, mixing until a soft dough forms.
Important: Stop kneading the moment the dough comes together. Over-kneaded dough makes hard koulourakia instead of crumbly ones.
Resting: Cover the dough and rest it for 30 minutes at room temperature — not in the fridge, or it becomes too stiff to shape.
Shaping: Roll pieces into ropes and form twists, plaits or rings, keeping them all the same thickness so they bake evenly.
Brushing: Brush with beaten egg yolk and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Baking: Bake at 180°C for 20-25 minutes until golden. Important: they firm up as they cool, so take them out while still slightly soft or they turn rock hard.
koulourakia_portokaliou.plate: Serve on a platter or in a glass jar, with coffee alongside.

steps: Choosing the butter: Use real butter, not margarine. Important: in a recipe this plain, the butter is the entire flavour — there is nothing to hide behind.
Softening: Leave the butter out until it yields to finger pressure but is not melted or oily.
Beating: Beat it with the sugar for 6 minutes, until genuinely white and doubled in volume.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla, milk and salt.
Adding the flour: Sift in the flour with the baking powder and mix until a soft, non-sticky dough forms.
Resting: Rest the dough for 20 minutes so the flour hydrates and it becomes easier to shape.
Shaping: Roll into ropes about 1.5 cm thick and shape into S-forms, rings or twists.
Important: Do not make them too thick. Butter koulourakia spread as they bake, and thick ones stay raw in the middle.
Brushing: Brush with egg yolk thinned with a little milk, for an even golden shine.
Baking: Bake at 180°C for 20 minutes, and cool them on a rack so the bottoms do not soften from trapped steam.
koulourakia_voutyrou.plate: Arrange fanned out on a platter, dusted with icing sugar.

steps: Chopping the chocolate: Chop a bar of chocolate by hand into uneven chunks instead of using chips. Important: hand-cut pieces melt into pools, while chips are designed to hold their shape and stay solid.
Browning the butter: Melt the butter over medium heat until it foams and small brown flecks appear at the bottom, smelling of hazelnuts. This step alone doubles the depth of flavour.
Cooling: Let the browned butter cool for 10 minutes. Important: hot butter cooks the egg on contact and turns the dough greasy.
Mixing the sugars: Beat the butter with both sugars for 2 minutes. The brown sugar gives chewiness, the white gives crisp edges.
Adding the egg: Beat in the egg and the vanilla until the mixture turns glossy.
Combining: Fold in the flour, soda and salt with a spatula, then the chocolate, mixing as little as possible.
Important: Chill the dough for at least 1 hour. Unchilled dough spreads into thin flat discs in the oven.
Shaping: Roll into balls and place them well apart on the tray — they spread to nearly double their width.
Baking: Bake at 180°C for 10-12 minutes only. The centres should still look underdone when you take them out.
Important: They finish cooking on the hot tray. Baking until they look done in the oven gives hard, dry biscuits.
biskota_sokolatas.plate: Serve warm, while the chocolate chips are still soft.

steps: Sifting the cocoa: Sift the cocoa together with the flour twice. Important: cocoa clumps stubbornly and unsifted lumps leave dry bitter pockets in the dough.
Beating the butter: Beat the butter with the sugar for 5 minutes until light.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.
Making the dough: Add the sifted dry ingredients gradually with the milk, mixing to a soft dough.
Important: Cocoa absorbs more liquid than flour. If the dough feels dry and cracks, add milk a spoonful at a time — never all at once.
Resting: Rest the dough for 30 minutes so it hydrates fully.
Shaping: Roll into ropes and form twists or rings, all the same size.
Important: Do not brush these with egg. On a dark dough the glaze is invisible, and the sugar in the yolk burns before the biscuit is done.
Baking: Bake at 175°C for 18-20 minutes — slightly lower than usual, because the dark colour hides burning until it is too late.
Testing: They are ready when the base is firm and they lift cleanly off the tray. Dust with icing sugar once cold.
koulourakia_kakao.plate: Serve on a platter dusted with icing sugar for contrast with the dark colour.

steps: Toasting the almonds: Toast the ground almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes until they smell fragrant, then let them cool completely. Important: raw ground almond tastes flat, and toasting is what wakes the flavour.
Beating the butter: Beat the butter with the sugar for 5 minutes.
Adding the egg: Add the egg and the almond extract and beat until smooth.
Combining: Mix in the flour, the cooled ground almonds and the baking powder to a soft dough.
Important: Ground almond carries fat but no gluten, so this dough is more fragile than usual. Handle it gently and do not knead it.
Chilling: Chill the dough for 30 minutes so the butter firms up and it holds its shape.
Shaping: Roll into balls and flatten them slightly, or form the traditional crescent shape.
Decorating: Press a whole almond into the centre of each and brush with lightly beaten egg white.
Baking: Bake at 170°C for 20-22 minutes. Important: keep the temperature low — ground almond burns far faster than flour and turns bitter.
Cooling: Leave them on the tray for 5 minutes before moving them, because they are very fragile while hot.
koulourakia_amygdalou.wine: Amaretto or a sweet white wine.
koulourakia_amygdalou.plate: Serve on a platter with whole almonds scattered between them.

steps: Warming the honey: Warm the honey gently until it flows freely. Important: never let it boil — high heat destroys its aroma and leaves only sweetness behind.
Mixing the liquids: Whisk the warm honey with the olive oil, the orange juice and the sugar until combined.
Adding the spices: Stir in the cinnamon and cloves, which need the liquid to distribute evenly.
Making the dough: Add the sifted flour with the baking powder gradually, mixing to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Important: Honey dough is always stickier than butter dough. Do not add extra flour to fix it — oil your hands instead.
Resting: Rest the dough for 20 minutes.
Shaping: Shape into small ropes or ovals with oiled hands and press sesame seeds onto the surface.
Baking: Bake at 180°C for 20 minutes.
Important: Watch them closely from minute 15. Honey caramelises and burns much faster than sugar, and they go from golden to black quickly.
Finishing: Drizzle with a little extra warm honey while still hot, so it soaks in rather than sitting on the surface.
koulourakia_meliou.plate: Serve drizzled with a little honey and sprinkled with sesame seeds.

steps: Preparing the vanilla: Split the pods lengthwise and scrape out the seeds with a knife tip. Important: real pods give a depth and speckled look that no extract can match.
Infusing the sugar: Rub the vanilla seeds into the sugar with your fingertips, so the aroma spreads through every grain.
Beating: Beat the butter with the vanilla sugar for 6 minutes until white and airy.
Adding the eggs: Add the eggs one at a time, then the milk.
Making the dough: Sift in the flour with the baking powder and salt and mix to a soft dough.
Resting: Rest for 30 minutes.
Shaping: Roll into ropes and form small rings or S-shapes, keeping them small — these are meant to be delicate.
Baking: Bake at 175°C for 18 minutes. Important: they must stay pale. Browning masks the vanilla, which is the whole point of the biscuit.
Dusting while warm: Roll them in icing sugar while still warm, so the first coat sticks and melts into the surface.
Second coat: Once cold, roll them a second time so they end up properly white.
koulourakia_vanilias.plate: Serve on a platter with plenty of icing sugar on top.

steps: Whisking the liquids: Whisk the olive oil with the sugar and the orange juice until they emulsify and thicken slightly.
Adding the eggs: Beat in the eggs, keeping one yolk aside for brushing.
Making the dough: Add the sifted flour with the baking powder and the spices, mixing to a firm, pliable dough.
Kneading: Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Important: unlike koulourakia, paximadakia want a well-kneaded dough — they need to hold together through two bakings.
Shaping the logs: Form long logs about 6 cm wide and flatten them slightly on the tray.
Brushing: Brush with the reserved yolk and press sesame seeds all over the surface.
First bake: Bake at 180°C for 30 minutes, until firm and golden.
Important: Take them out and let them cool for 15 minutes before slicing. Hot logs crumble under the knife; cooled ones cut cleanly.
Slicing: Cut into slices about 1.5 cm thick with a serrated knife, using a sawing motion.
Second bake: Lay the slices cut-side up and bake again at 150°C for 25-30 minutes, until completely dry. This second low bake is what makes them keep for weeks.
paximadakia_elaioladou.plate: Serve in a basket or glass jar — they keep for weeks.

steps: Mixing the dry ingredients: Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt together in a bowl.
Mixing the wet ingredients: Beat the eggs with the milk, the melted butter and the vanilla in a second bowl.
Combining: Pour the wet into the dry and stir 10 times only, with a spoon.
Important: The batter must stay lumpy. Every extra stir develops gluten, and gluten turns pancakes flat and rubbery.
Resting: Rest the batter for 15 minutes. The baking powder starts working and bubbles form on the surface — this is what gives the height.
Heating the pan: Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little butter using kitchen paper.
Important: Medium heat, never high. On a hot pan the outside burns while the inside stays raw batter.
Cooking: Pour a ladle per pancake and wait until bubbles appear over the whole surface and the edges look set — about 2 minutes.
Flipping: Flip once and cook for 1 minute more. Important: flip only once — a second flip deflates them.
Keeping warm: Stack them on a plate under a clean tea towel, which keeps them warm and soft while you cook the rest.
american_pancakes.plate: Stack 3-4 in a tower with maple syrup running down and butter on top.

steps: Preparing the blueberries: Wash the blueberries and dry them very well on kitchen paper.
Important: Wet blueberries burst and bleed purple through the batter, turning the pancakes grey.
Flouring: Toss them in a tablespoon of the measured flour so they stay suspended instead of sinking.
Making the batter: Mix the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ones in another, then combine with 10 stirs only.
Resting: Rest the batter for 15 minutes.
Important: Do not stir the blueberries into the batter. Instead, drop them onto each pancake after it is in the pan — this keeps them whole and evenly spread.
Cooking: Pour a ladle into the pan over medium heat and scatter 6-8 blueberries over the surface.
Waiting: Cook until bubbles cover the surface and the edges set, about 2 minutes.
Flipping: Flip carefully — the fruit makes them heavier and more fragile than plain pancakes.
Finishing: Cook for 1 minute more and serve at once, while the blueberries are still hot and bursting.
pancakes_myrtila.plate: Serve stacked with fresh blueberries scattered over and maple syrup.

steps: Choosing the bananas: Use bananas with brown-spotted skins — they are sweeter and mash to a smooth pulp.
Mashing: Mash them thoroughly with a fork until almost no lumps remain, so they blend into the batter rather than forming pockets.
Mixing the wet ingredients: Whisk the mashed banana with the eggs, the milk and the melted butter.
Mixing the dry ingredients: Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, cinnamon and salt separately.
Combining: Pour the wet into the dry and stir just until incorporated, leaving lumps.
Important: This batter is thicker than plain pancake batter because of the banana. Do not thin it with milk — the thickness is what makes them fluffy.
Resting: Rest for 10 minutes.
Cooking: Cook over medium-low heat. Important: the banana sugars caramelise and burn faster, so a lower heat than usual is essential.
Timing: Wait a little longer than with plain pancakes, about 3 minutes per side, since the thicker batter needs time to cook through.
Serving: Serve warm with banana slices and honey.
pancakes_banana.plate: Serve topped with banana slices and honey or peanut butter.

steps: Making the batter: Whisk the eggs with the milk, then add the flour gradually while whisking to avoid lumps.
Straining: Pass the batter through a sieve. Important: this single step removes every lump and is the difference between smooth crêpes and patchy ones.
Adding the butter: Whisk in the melted butter, the sugar and the salt.
Resting: Important: Rest the batter in the fridge for at least 1 hour. The flour hydrates and the gluten relaxes, which is what makes crêpes tender and easy to flip.
Checking the consistency: The batter should be as thin as single cream. If it has thickened while resting, loosen it with a little milk.
Heating the pan: Heat a crêpe pan over medium-high heat and wipe it with butter on kitchen paper — a thin film, never a pool.
First crêpe: Accept that the first one always fails. It calibrates the heat and seasons the pan.
Pouring: Pour a small ladle into the centre and immediately swirl the pan so the batter spreads into a thin even circle.
Cooking: Cook for about 1 minute, until the edges lift and the underside is golden, then flip and cook 30 seconds more.
Stacking: Stack them on a plate one on top of the other — the trapped steam keeps them soft and pliable.
krepes_klasikes.plate: Fold into triangles or rolls and dust with icing sugar and lemon.

steps: Preparing the batter: Make the classic crêpe batter and rest it for 1 hour.
Toasting the hazelnuts: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 4 minutes, then rub them in a towel to remove the skins and chop them coarsely.
Softening the spread: Warm the hazelnut spread slightly in a bowl set over warm water, or for 15 seconds in the microwave.
Important: Cold hazelnut spread tears the crêpe when you spread it. Warm, it glides on without damaging the surface.
Cooking the crêpes: Cook the crêpes over medium-high heat, about 1 minute per side.
Spreading: Spread the hazelnut spread while the crêpe is still warm in the pan or on the plate — the residual heat helps it spread thin and evenly.
Important: Leave a 2 cm clear border all around, or the filling squeezes out of the sides as you fold.
Adding the banana: Lay banana slices over half the surface.
Folding: Fold in half and then in half again into a triangle, or roll it into a cylinder.
Finishing: Scatter the toasted hazelnuts over, dust with icing sugar and serve immediately while the hazelnut spread is still molten.
krepes_nutella.plate: Fold into a triangle with the hazelnut spread spilling out and add chopped hazelnuts.

ing: Fresh yeast 20 g or dry 7 g
steps: Activating the yeast: Dissolve the yeast with the sugar in a little lukewarm water and leave it for 10 minutes until it foams.
Important: The water must be lukewarm, never hot. Above 45°C the yeast dies and the batter never rises.
Making the batter: Mix the flour with the salt, add the yeast mixture and the rest of the water, whisking to a smooth thick batter.
Rising: Cover the bowl with a towel and leave it in a warm spot for 1 hour, until it has doubled and the surface is covered in bubbles.
Important: Do not stir the batter after it has risen. Those bubbles are the whole structure — stirring collapses them and the tiganites come out flat.
Heating the oil: Heat plenty of oil in a deep pan to 175°C. Tiganites must float, so the oil should be at least 3 cm deep.
Testing: Drop in a little batter — it should rise to the surface immediately and puff up.
Frying: Drop in spoonfuls with an oiled spoon, without crowding the pan.
Cooking: Fry for 2 minutes per side, until deep golden and puffed, turning once.
Draining and serving: Drain on a rack and serve at once, drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon and chopped walnuts.
tiganites_ellinikes.plate: Serve piping hot, drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon and walnuts.

steps: Choosing the bread: Use thick slices of brioche or bread that is a day or two old. Important: fresh soft bread disintegrates in the custard and cannot be turned in the pan.
Making the custard: Beat the eggs with the milk, sugar, cinnamon, vanilla and salt until completely smooth.
Straining: Pass it through a sieve to catch the stringy bits of egg white, which would otherwise cook into rubbery threads on the surface.
Soaking: Dip each slice for 20 seconds per side. Important: no longer — over-soaked bread falls apart and stays wet in the middle.
Draining: Lift each slice and let the excess drip off before it goes into the pan.
Heating the pan: Heat a pan over medium-low heat with a knob of butter.
Important: Low heat and patience. On high heat the outside browns in seconds while the custard inside stays raw and eggy.
Cooking: Cook for 3 minutes per side, until deep golden and set right through.
Managing the butter: Wipe the pan and add fresh butter between batches — burnt butter turns the next slices bitter.
Serving: Serve immediately with maple syrup, fresh fruit and a dusting of cinnamon.
french_toast.plate: Serve in slices with maple syrup, fresh fruit and a pinch of cinnamon.

steps: Separating the eggs: Separate the yolks from the whites carefully. Important: a single drop of yolk in the whites stops them whipping — this is the step the whole recipe rests on.
Making the base: Whisk the yolks with the milk, the melted butter and the vanilla.
Mixing the dry ingredients: Combine the flour, cornflour, sugar, baking powder and salt. The cornflour is what gives waffles their crisp shell.
Combining: Fold the dry ingredients into the yolk mixture until just smooth.
Whipping the whites: Whip the egg whites to firm peaks in a spotlessly clean, dry bowl.
Important: Fold the whites in gently in three additions, with upward strokes. This trapped air is the difference between a waffle and a thick pancake.
Heating the iron: Heat the waffle iron thoroughly and brush it with butter or oil, even if it is non-stick.
Filling: Pour in enough batter to cover about three quarters of the surface — it expands as it cooks.
Important: Do not open the iron for the first 3 minutes. Opening early tears the waffle in half, because the crust has not set yet.
Cooking and serving: Cook for 4-5 minutes until golden and crisp, and serve at once — waffles soften within minutes of coming out.
waffle.plate: Serve warm with whipped cream, chocolate and fruit tucked into the squares.

steps: Grating the pumpkin: Peel the pumpkin, remove the seeds and grate it coarsely.

Important: Salt the grated pumpkin lightly and leave it in a colander for 1 hour, then squeeze it hard. Pumpkin is almost entirely water, and this is the only thing that saves the phyllo from going soggy.
Making the filling: Mix the drained pumpkin with the sugar, the rice, the chopped walnuts, the raisins, the cinnamon and the cloves.
Why the rice: The rice absorbs any liquid released during baking and keeps the filling from running.
Preparing the tin: Oil a large tin and lay in 4 phyllo sheets, brushing each one with oil.
Filling: Spread the filling evenly, leaving a small border at the edges.
Covering: Lay the remaining 4 sheets on top, brushing each with oil, and tuck the edges in neatly.
Important: Score the pie into portions before baking, cutting only the top layers. Scoring afterwards shatters the crisp phyllo.
Baking: Sprinkle a little water over the surface — this makes the phyllo blister and crisp — and bake at 180°C for 50-60 minutes.
Resting: Let it rest for 20 minutes, then dust with icing sugar and cinnamon and cut along the score lines.
kolokithopita_glykia.wine: A sweet wine or cinnamon tea.
kolokithopita_glykia.plate: Serve warm in pieces, dusted with icing sugar and cinnamon.

steps: Beat the butter and sugar until light and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time.
Sift together the flour, cocoa, and baking powder. Fold into the batter alternately with the milk, mixing gently.
Pour into a buttered baking pan and bake at 175°C for 45 minutes.
Beat the eggs and sugar until light and fluffy. Add the olive oil, yogurt, lemon zest, and lemon juice.
Sift the flour and baking powder and fold in gently.
Bake at 175°C for 40 minutes. Drizzle with lemon glaze.
Beat the eggs and sugar. Gradually add the olive oil, orange juice, and zest.
Sift the flour and baking powder and fold in gently.
Bake at 180°C for 45 minutes.
Mash the bananas. Beat the butter and sugar, then add the eggs and mashed bananas.
Sift the flour, baking soda, and baking powder. Fold in gently.
Bake at 175°C for 55 minutes in a loaf pan.
Beat the eggs and sugar. Add the olive oil and grated carrots.
Sift the flour, cinnamon, nutmeg, and baking powder. Fold in gently.
Bake at 175°C for 50 minutes. Top with cream cheese frosting.
Beat the butter and sugar. Add the eggs one at a time. Alternate adding the flour and milk.
Divide the batter in two, and stir the cocoa into one half.
Spoon the two batters into the pan in alternating dollops. Bake at 175°C for 50 minutes.
Beat the butter and sugar. Add the eggs and yogurt.
Sift the flour and baking powder. Fold in along with the chopped strawberries.
Bake at 175°C for 45 minutes.
Beat the eggs, sugar, olive oil, and yogurt together.
Sift the flour, cinnamon, and baking powder. Add the grated apples.
Bake at 175°C for 50 minutes.
Beat the butter and sugar. Add the eggs, orange juice, and zest.
Sift the flour and baking powder. Knead lightly.
Shape the cookies and bake at 175°C for 15-18 minutes.
Beat the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy. Add the eggs and vanilla.
Sift in the flour. Knead gently.
Pipe with a piping bag or shape by hand, then bake at 170°C for 18-20 minutes.
